e1c16679cd.title: NeuroFusion Tops AI Future-Forecasting Benchmark, Beating Google and OpenAI
e1c16679cd.summary: South Korean financial AI company NeuroFusion has risen to the top of a benchmark testing the future-forecasting abilities of global artificial intelligence (AI) models, beating big-tech models from Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. NeuroFusion said on the 20th that its financial AI research team ranked No. 1 on the overall leaderboard of ForecastBench, a benchmark for predicting the probability of future events. As of the 17th of this month, its overall Brier Index stood at 69.4 points, the highest among the 550 models evaluated. This follows its earlier first-place finish on the preliminary dataset leaderboard in September, and it has now secured the top spot in the official rankings as well. ForecastBench is operated by the Forecasting Research Institute (FRI), which includes Philip Tetlock, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, among its participants, and is an evaluation framework accepted to the international conference ICLR 2025. Because it compares probability forecasts for questions whose outcomes are not yet determined at the time of submission against actual results, it fundamentally prevents answer leakage or performance inflation from pre-training. The evaluation is divided into a dataset category covering economic and financial indicators such as corporate stock prices, US Treasury yields and policy rates, and a market category covering events requiring qualitative judgment, such as major-country election outcomes and whether international conflict negotiations are concluded. The overall ranking weights the two categories equally, and results are only recognized as official records after 50 days have passed since the forecast was submitted and the outcome has been confirmed. NeuroFusion scored 65.5 points in the dataset category and 73.9 points in the market category. The gap with competing models is also clear. Google DeepMind, which submitted its model directly, trailed by 1.0 point at 68.4, while NeuroFusion widened its lead by 2.5 to 3.4 points over xAI's "Grok 4.20" (66.9), which was evaluated by organizers with web search applied, OpenAI's "GPT-6 Astra" (66.7), Anthropic's "Claude Opus 5.5" (66.6) and Meta's "Muse Spark 1.3" (66.0). Converted to a difficulty-adjusted Brier score, NeuroFusion's "Seraphine AI" reduced forecast error by 15-16% compared with the comparison models from Anthropic and OpenAI. af11a2b676.summary: Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit OpenAI has revised the terms for its new ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch. The change came after Digiday reported that lawyers viewed the original language as potentially limiting businesses’ ability to bring certain legal claims against the company. Launched last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics. For publishers, it’s a first-party view of activity they’ve largely had to estimate. Before the revision, Section 10 of OpenAI’s terms of service for businesses using ChatGPT appeared to require those businesses to give up certain legal claims against OpenAI, lawyers told Digiday. They said the language could apply to claims involving content published on their websites, before they signed up. Alan Chapell, privacy expert and founder of Chapell and Associates, said publishers who signed up for ChatGPT’s Business Hub and accepted the terms could have faced restrictions on how they pursued such claims against OpenAI. The terms included a mandatory arbitration provision and class-action waiver, potentially requiring businesses to resolve disputes individually and outside of court, Chapell said. The provision was broadly worded to cover certain claims that arose before the agreement was accepted, he explained. Businesses had 30 days to opt out of arbitration, but if they did not, they could have faced limits on their ability to obtain evidence, pursue appeals and establish legal precedent through public court proceedings, Chapell added. This could’ve put a chokehold on publishers that are in the midst of figuring out how to protect and monetize their content in the AI era, potentially limiting their ability to bring copyright infringement claims against OpenAI down the road. Hours after Digiday first contacted OpenAI on Nov. 18, the terms were revised. They now include a waiver of businesses’ rights to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data, according to an IP and tech lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “There are still some restrictions here but they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse. eb42bbb391.title: Asia’s stock markets dive as Anthropic debut fails to allay AI bubble fears
eb42bbb391.summary: Asian stock markets have opened with steep losses as fears that the AI boom is unsustainable persist despite Anthropic’s blockbuster debut. Markets in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fell sharply on Friday, as investor excitement around the Claude creator’s public listing failed to allay concerns about the sustainability of the multi-trillion-dollar investments propping up AI. Tokyo’s benchmark Nikkei 225 tumbled as much as 4.9 percent, while Seoul’s Kospi fell 5.4 percent. In Taipei, the Taiex plunged more than 6.8 percent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index dipped more than 2 percent. The sell-off reflects concerns that AI-led growth is slowing down and the “peak growth phase” may have passed, said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist with Societe Generale. “The second element is on the demand vacuum that we are seeing,” Agarwal told Al Jazeera. “At the time when foreigners are not buying, it is to be seen how long can the domestic investors stay put, particularly in Korea, on which the drawdown has been more severe.” Like Wall Street, Asia’s main bourses are heavily exposed to AI. The region is home to some of the key players in the global AI ecosystem, including South Korean memory chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, Taiwanese contract chipmaker TSMC, and Japanese investment holding company SoftBank Group. Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI in recent years in anticipation of future profits, stoking fears of a debt-fuelled market bubble reminiscent of the splurge that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash. Global AI-related investment is projected to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner. Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at Union Bancaire Privee in Hong Kong, said the sell-off in multiple markets reflected a “collapse in confidence in the AI investment thesis”. “Global technology stocks have retreated throughout the week, with Asia’s chip-heavy markets bearing the brunt of the sell-off,” Casanova told Al Jazeera. “Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO did little to ease broader concerns about the outlook for AI-related equities and may, if anything, have crystallised the debate,” he said. “Rather than lifting the broader AI complex, the listing appears to have diverted liquidity from established AI plays as investors rotated into the new issue,” he added. “Nvidia’s earnings earlier this week also failed to provide the reassurance markets were seeking.”…

Agencies in Santa Ana, Brea, Anaheim, Garden Grove and Laguna Hills were affected, causing residents in those cities to experience delays in receiving their benefits. Microsoft 365 experienced a widespread outage after its servers failed “automated health checks” and became unavailable on Nov. 12, according to the company’s status updates on X . Among the services disrupted were Microsoft Teams and Outlook, which are used by the agencies. Chi Pham, the Public Information Officer for Orange County’s Social Service Agency, said that agency employees were not able to help clients in a timely manner due to disrupted access to the system. Two to three employees remained outside the facility to help visitors seeking assistance with obtaining new cards or replacements, but staff could not verify the client’s eligibility or current benefits. Emergency services were not affected. If residents wanted to apply for any type of benefits they were not able to submit applications online. Instead applications had to be filled out and submitted by hand, causing a backlog at the Santa Ana regional center. Pham reported that the total number of applications received across all agencies on Thursday was “roughly 2,000.” The outage also prevented family violence workers from accessing databases containing client information, according to. When Microsoft’s systems experience disruptions, the applications and services relying on them can also become unavailable. Service disruptions continued into the following day, Nov. 13 Downdetector , a website that tracks user reports of service disruptions, reported continued issues with Microsoft 365. Its status page identified Outlook and email as the primary sources of reported problems, with additional disruptions affecting Teams, Copilot and other applications. By Nov. 13 at 8:52 a.m., Downdetector had received 1,233 reports of Microsoft 365 services still not working, a significant decrease from the 46,586 reports recorded on Nov. 12 at 10:22 a.m. Although Downdetector reports decreased significantly between Nov. 12 and Nov. 13, users continued reporting problems accessing Microsoft 365 services. 40079238b1.summary: Last month, Microsoft asked as many as 60,000 employees to voluntarily leave their jobs with buyout offers. This week, CEO Satya Nadella took some time to explain why. In a talk with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the New York Times ' DealBook Summit in New York City (as reported by TechCrunch ), Nadella addressed the buyout offer that made headlines in October. As we reported at the time, the buyouts came amidst a huge amount of AI investment at Microsoft and industry-wide AI layoffs . And in his comments at the summit, Nadella made it explicitly clear that the company reorganization was necessary because of AI. You can listen to the CEO's full comments at about 27:20 in the New York Times' YouTube video of the interview : According to Nadella, it's not necessarily about directly replacing humans with AI in a one-to-one fashion. However, that may not be comforting to workers asked to leave their jobs, if only voluntarily. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile “Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” Nadella said. Like many tech leaders, Nadella believes the future of development at Microsoft and beyond involves humans managing a team of AI agents, an approach that many Big Tech companies have already adopted. For example, the team behind the Microsoft 365 AI agent Cowork consists of only 11 human beings who, in Nadella's words, "build a software factory that builds the product" rather than writing the product code themselves. Rather than simply laying off workers, Nadella said the buyouts were intended to give workers some measure of control over their future at Microsoft. By opting for buyouts, the CEO said that he wanted “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," per TechCrunch. b670d8fae4.title: Anthropic Stock Is Down 13% From Its Opening Price. Is This Dip Worth Buying?
b670d8fae4.summary: Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) stock had a surprisingly lackluster first day of trading . While its opening price of $111.50 per share was well above its $83 per share IPO price, and it briefly headed toward almost $115, the stock began to slide within minutes. By the close of trading, it was at $97.17 per share — 13% below the opening price. Given that performance, investors may want to consider buying the stock, albeit with a more cautious approach. Admittedly, many stocks gain ground quickly at their debut. This is especially true of well-known businesses like Anthropic, whose Claude AI Assistant has become a top choice for many users. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Moreover, at a market cap of $1.76 trillion as of the time of this writing, Anthropic is now trading at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of around 50. Although that amounts to a significant premium, investors might be willing to pay it given the company's 1,127% revenue growth in the third quarter. Assuming Anthropic's rapid growth continues for a few more quarters, the stock could actually be a bargain. However, investors need to remember that the purpose of IPOs is to raise money, meaning they tend to occur well into bull markets. This often sets such stocks up for steep declines when the broader sentiment turns bearish, which is why these stocks can end up trading below their IPO prices for extended periods. Additionally, the sell-off that took place after its brief early surge suggests that investors have less appetite for this SaaS stock than they did for Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX). SpaceX debuted in June and surged by as much as 49% above its IPO price in its first few trading days before pulling back to well below that level over the following month. Human-level intelligence is merely one node on the broader spectrum of intelligence, with enormous capability space still above it. DeepMind notes that how much capability space exists between human-level AGI and the theoretical limit remains an insufficiently explored question. 7bc8377aab.title: Anthropic's IPO ties the fate of the US economy closer to AI
7bc8377aab.summary: The day finally arrived. Anthropic ( ANT ) began trading on Thursday at $111.50 per share, surging above its $83 IPO price and briefly attaining a market capitalization of $2 trillion before settling into a still-respectable $1.2 trillion. What took years for the tech giants to achieve, the frontier AI lab grabbed in an instant . But the historic IPO is notable not just for its size , but also for what it says — and will say — about the makeup of the stock market and the outsized influence of its largest players. The top 10 biggest companies make up close to 40% of the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ). A bad day for tech means a bad day for the market. And now that Anthropic has joined the trillion-dollar ticker club — though it won't join the S&P 500 anytime soon — Wall Street's fate is tightly bound with another huge tech company, which also happens to be an AI lab without a long track record of financial stability. The top-heavy nature of the S&P 500 means the benchmark index is less diverse than it looks. Sure, investors are buying into a basket of hundreds of names. But since the tickers with the largest market caps get the highest proportional weights, a handful of names can move the entire index. That's how you can get such different performances from the equal-weighted S&P 500 ( ^SPXEW ) index (up 11% so far this year) versus the standard, market-weighted version (up 6%). 8332c3a79c.summary: Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Artificial intelligence could soon pass through an important threshold – and we should start thinking about what it might mean, researchers at Google DeepMind have warned. For years, AI researchers and commentators have been looking ahead to artificial general intelligence, or AGI, which refers to proposed machines that would match human performance across nearly all cognitive tasks. But that prospect is now coming in reach, and could be followed shortly after by artificial general superintelligence, or ASI, according to Tim Genewein, a research scientist at Google DeepMind . That could bring machines that are able to perform better than large numbers of humans on a wide variety of tasks, such as making scientific progress across a whole research field in a short amount of time, or similarly grand achievements in practical tasks such as chip design. Importantly, ASI could only be said to have happened when computers are able to reach that standard across nearly all tasks that are of interest to humans – rather than just in specific ways, as has arguably already happened now. Some critics are skeptical that even AGI could actually happen. They argue that there are fundamental barriers to the capabilities of the AI systems we have today, such as the fact that most of them operate largely through language, which means that they are limited in what they can know about the actual world. But in a new blog post, Mr Genewein argues that a process of “cognitive industrialisation” will lead to dramatically more powerful AI systems. That will be driven by improvements in hardware design of the chips that power AI systems, better efficiency in the systems themselves, as well as the vast investment in new hardware – all of which, taken together, means that the effective amount of computer processing power available for artificial intelligence work is growing by ten times each year, which adds up to an improvement of 10 billion times over ten years. But while that improvement might bring AGI, or human-level capabilities to AI, it does not necessarily mean that machines will not hit limits that will stop the progress of ASI. Mr Genewein compared it with the fact that Albert Einstein was able to find general relativity, while even a thousand astronomers from the ancient world working together would not have been able to do so. In a November 18 report , the company estimated that the success rate rose from 23% in March to 46% in October. The findings, covered in The Rundown , show how much work the lab is handing to agents as it develops new models. OpenAI also reported that success on tasks requiring four to eight human hours rose from 13% to 35% over the same period. The trend has a caveat. OpenAI’s task mix changed, so stronger models and better choices about what to delegate could both explain the improvement. For October, OpenAI valued median agent usage at $2,400 per researcher per day, based on API list prices. A survey of 101 people also found that the median respondent would hypothetically trade 40% of their team’s headcount for three months of access to frontier agents. Daily runtime averaged 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, counting each workday as eight hours. That was an elevenfold increase. More than two thirds of researchers averaged daily peaks of at least four agents running at once. Runtime measures activity, so it says little on its own about the quality of the output. Interviewees still criticized agents’ research judgment and complained about “AI slop.” They credited humans with the sampled ideas behind GPT-6 Astra, while saying Codex helped generate key pretraining insights for GPT-6.2 Astra. f295b3ea96.summary: The long goodbye has begun. At this year’s Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, The National spoke to Emirates chief operating officer Adel Al Redha about the future of the Airbus A380, the so-called superjumbo of the skies. “We have a plan to operate the A380 until maybe 2035 or 2040,” Mr Al Redha said. “There will be a phase-out because we can only operate the aircraft up to a certain limit, because it becomes very difficult to maintain it and very expensive to operate it. We are sad not to have this aircraft to operate with us forever,” he said. Emirates is the largest operator of A380s by some margin, accounting for about half of the 250 superjumbos built. The airline took delivery of the last A380 off the production line in December 2021. Much, but not all, of the capacity will be taken over by the airline’s fleet of Boeing 777s when the superjumbo is retired, he said. When The National put details of the interview on social media, users flooded our post with comments. What was, perhaps, more unusual was they wrote near-universal positive comments about the aircraft. Social media is rarely so united in its praise for anything. “Best passenger experience ever,” wrote one. “The comfort is unbeatable,” commented another. “Nothing compares to it,” one person said. “Every other aircraft is a downgrade,” said another. The comments stretched on and on in a form of the most benevolent infinite scroll. “There is no better than the A380,” a further comment read. “Let it run forever. Best cabin. Best plane,” another said. Space does not permit a full expurgation of what was written, but those words paint an accurate picture of the depth of overwhelmingly goodwill the superjumbo generates. Much-loved and much-admired might be the best description. Such positive consumer reactions to the superjumbo may explain why some other airlines are reimagining their fleet. British Airways said this month that it will update its A380s with a new large business class cabin that uses the entire upper deck of the aircraft. Despite this, the direction of travel is clear. The aircraft, which began commercial operations in October 2007, will be all but gone by 2040, a significantly shorter span of time than the 747 and not much longer than Concorde. The comparisons are intentional. Both Concorde and the original jumbo were equally beloved by those who used them. 048307fe18.title: OpenAI helped AMD improve its upcoming flagship GPU design by 14% PPA — GPT models also helping Lisa Su's outfit boost its new CPUs
048307fe18.summary: OpenAI just revealed new details about its ongoing partnership with AMD, in which engineers used undisclosed AI models to help optimize the hardware maker's upcoming flagship GPU and CPU designs. The leading figures are up to 14% PPA (power, performance, and area) improvement for the GPU circuitry, and unspecified single-digit PPA gains on the processor. OpenAI says that its model spotted "further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits." This work was done in SystemVerilog RTL, the language commonly used for high-end chip design. The firm claims that its model's optimization efforts are equivalent to condensing a year's worth of conventional chip design work into "under 5 months" — a time crunch it says is unprecedented in this arena. Furthermore, OpenAI says its model was reasoning on RTL "at the level of an expert microarchitect," and that it expects to squeeze further PPA improvements in both GPU and CPU designs, up from the now-improved baseline. This isn't AI's first time working on chips. It worked with Broadcom on designing OpenAI Jalapeño, an inference-targeted chip that was already running actual workloads with engineering samples as far back as June 2026. The company expected to have small initial Jalapeño deployments around late 2026, and pinned a broader rollout to 2027. Test benchmarks have been out for a while, displaying purported excellent savings on power draw and overall latency versus the market-leading Nvidia Blackwell GPUs in single-token prediction workloads. The blog post also explains how GPT's chip-design acumen evolved. The researchers tested its high-end LLMs by asking them to improve PicoRV32 and Ibex chip cores. The models were given 112,000 tokens per run, told to optimize for throughput (a combination of Instructions-per-Clock and clock-cycle duration), and scored the results. A fat zero was given if the chips didn't work or used more than 16x the previous area, and 1.0 was given for the best designs under the test constraints. The test also didn't tell the models which workloads the chips were going to be used for. As expected, GPT-6.2 Astra had by far the best showing, on both axes: both the lowest overall cost and the highest optimization score. The six consecutive declining S&P 500 sessions mark the index’s longest losing streak since April 2024. A seventh losing day would make it the longest stretch since the pandemic slump in February 2020, according to Deutsche Bank. For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove stubborn. Given the importance the AI trade has played this year in propelling markets and economic growth writ large, its derailment amid concerns about costs, debt, profitability and political risk could have broader implications. Investor concerns about AI revenues tied to exports of advanced technology to China compounded the sell-off. The Jensen Huang scandal pulling down Nvidia appeared to broaden Thursday, when a short-selling firm issued a report raising questions about whether Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, may also have had shipments to Asia diverted to mainland China. Alongside the stock sell-off, there has been an increase in purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeing signs of weakening growth amid higher interest rates from the Federal Reserve and a stalling economy in China. “The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday. Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation. “They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. 3f3ebbe6f0.title: Why Anthropic’s blockbuster debut didn’t ease Wall Street’s AI fears
3f3ebbe6f0.summary: Anthropic’s IPO went better than expected . Demand was hot, Wall Street jumped at its first chance to buy in to a frontier AI model. The stock got a nice bounce. What a relief for the beaten-down AI industry? Not exactly. The rest of the tech stock market wasn’t invited to Anthropic’s party on Thursday. The Nasdaq slumped. Again. Friday looks like more of the same: The Nasdaq fell 2.6% and is now down for the year. Even Anthropic’s stock is down 10% in early trading Friday – a consequence of getting swept up in the AI malaise that’s been brewing for six straight weeks … and the fact that its underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley aren’t working quite as hard to prop up the stock like they did on Thursday. Buying shares of Anthropic is a wager on the future of AI , a bet that the AI-fueled economy will someday soon transition from investment in construction sites to profit generated from customers paying for large language models to revolutionize research, medicine, manufacturing and the way the world works. That bet may pay off big time. But in the here and now, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO didn’t change the narrative that has been worrying Wall Street since early October: Regulation could be around the corner, AI investment may slow down, valuations are sky high , and some of the early bets placed on the transformative technology may fail to pay off. AI has been on wobbly footing since October 6, when the market last hit a record. Since then, the AI-spending-will-just-keep-growing-forever narrative has absorbed blow after blow. CoreWeave. It started when CoreWeave’s bond yields rose to 15% (when the company’s return on investment was only 9%). That sent alarm bells ringing that maybe some parts of the AI industry were valued way too high — particularly neoclouds like CoreWeave that buy computing power at high prices and lease it out to other companies. 9aea482b13.title: Successive technology outages complicate classes for MSU students, professors
9aea482b13.summary: A week of cascading tech failures hit Michigan State University students where it hurts most: their inboxes. After a Microsoft Outlook outage, a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration groundstop and a software bug at JPMorgan Chase knocked out online banking across the country last week, successive outages across various digital platforms have complicated day-to-day operations for students and faculty alike. Human resources management freshman Bella Greene woke up sick the morning of the Microsoft Outlook outage on Nov. 12, so she emailed her professor to say she wouldn't make it to class and went back to sleep, assuming her message went through. When Greene woke up later, it was to a notification for a "non-revocable absence." The email never went through. The outage "sucked," Greene said, and there was nothing to warn her. Greene had no idea her email wasn't sending, so she had no reason to try another way. During the Microsoft Outlook outage, an MSU announcement said Spartan Mail was experiencing issues and warned that other Office 365 applications may be unavailable or delayed. MSU also updated its service status monitor and maintenance calendar so students and staff could track Spartan Mail performance and check for updates, although Greene didn't learn her email had stopped working until the absence showed up on her record. Landscape architecture freshman Sarah Shafto ran into a different wall. Shafto and her classmates "couldn't see the slides our professor posted" on D2L, and with Microsoft Outlook down, there was no way to reach out for help. "It was really stressful," Shafto said. "Nothing would load and it was difficult to study and complete assignments." For business professor Scott Hamric, the timing of the outage was especially awkward. Hamric had scheduled a professional career panel during class so students could learn the basics of supply chain management from people actually working in the field. Since it ran on Zoom, the panel itself survived, but the Microsoft Outlook outage was still worrisome because the panelists were professionals giving up valuable time, and any technical disruption would have wasted it. The instructional team for BUS 100, Business Major and Career Exploration, felt the ramifications of Microsoft Outlook being down immediately. The team alerted students through D2L that they would "respond to emails as soon as email access is restored." Access would be restored around 24 hours after Microsoft Outlook users…

5deb1a157a.title: Virginia Sen. Mark Warner warns of more outages after disruptions hit banks, airlines, and federal agencies
5deb1a157a.summary: A series of major technology outages struck systems millions of Americans rely on — from bank accounts to air travel — and Virginia Sen. Mark Warner is warning there could be more disruptions ahead. Over the course of just a few days, some of the country’s most critical systems went offline. Warner says there is no evidence the outages were the result of cyberattacks. Instead, he says new artificial intelligence tools are finding security weaknesses faster than companies can fix them — creating a race to update software that some systems simply aren’t built to handle. “You can almost think about it as leaks and pipes. Not a direct analogy. But where it used to be you’d have one leak a month or every three months. You may have a hundred leaks in a single day,” Warner said. “And if you’re suddenly trying to put all of the patches on at once, you’re not, in some cases, testing the patches quick enough.” Warner says the FAA ground stop was a separate issue — tied to equipment upgrades rather than artificial intelligence. Still, he says the broader pattern of outages is cause for concern. While the security updates are meant to make systems safer in the long run, Warner warns the public should brace for continued disruptions as companies scramble to make the changes AI is detecting. “So, we are going to go through a period of, I fear, outages as companies try to patch quickly,” Warner said. “At the end of the day, our systems will be safer.” Beyond the outages themselves, Warner says the bigger risk may be what happens to public confidence in artificial intelligence if the disruptions continue — or get worse. “And my fear is that I think there are still enormous value coming from artificial intelligence and innovation and productivity,” Warner said. “But should we have more of these outages without warning? Or God forbid we have a rogue AI agent go out and do things the way the open AI agent went against this company hugging phase. Or we have an AI-generated cyber-attack, then I think the American people are going to say, hey, we’re done with this. We don’t want to take these risks. So let’s put a risk system in place.” Warner says establishing a risk framework for AI is a priority. Copyright 2026 by WSLS 10 - All rights reserved.

d31324a1ec.title: Will Al Zaidi’s show of force for Jurf Al Sakhar pay off?
d31324a1ec.summary: A tense stand-off between Iraqi troops and a powerful Iran-backed militia in the town of Jurf Al Sakhar , south of Baghdad, eased off at the 11th hour this week. The town has long been controlled by Kataib Hezbollah , from where the militia has been accused of smuggling oil. But a recently leaked intelligence report alleging theft has put the government under pressure to act. Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi gave Kataib Hezbollah until today to withdraw but before the deadline expired, a compromise was reached. Instead, Iraq’s security arms would jointly be deployed to secure the area. It comes as Baghdad faces increasing pressure from Washington to bring armed groups under state control. But Tehran, too, has much sway in the country. For now, a more serious confrontation has been averted, but the power dynamics have not yet changed. In this episode of Beyond the Headlines , host Nada AlTaher discusses the significance of Jurf Al Sakhar and asks whether Mr Al Zaidi’s show of force would pay off or backfire. She speaks to Michael Knights, head of research at Horizon Engage and adjunct fellow at The Washington Institute, and The National ’s foreign editor, Mohamad Ali Harisi.

It wasn’t enough to keep the rest of the market from going the other way on Thursday. The Dow fell 1,101 points , or 2.19%, to 49,097, and closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. The S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq lost 2.2%. The selling spread to Asia and Europe overnight, Fortune ’s Jim Edwards reported . Anthropic slid 11% on Friday, for a stock price around $86, while the Nasdaq lost 1.55% and the S&P 500 was down 0.5%. The stakes go well past one stock. AI capital spending produced “about half” of S&P 500 earnings growth this year, according to Goldman Sachs Research, and Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI investment boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. If you own an index fund, you own a bet on the data-center buildout. James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics , wrote Friday that the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 “have further to run.” The success of Anthropic’s IPO as other AI-related stocks tumbled, he wrote, “highlights how different parts of the AI ecosystem no longer move as one.” That split already shows up in prices. 8d4aa7c610.summary: Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) 's strategy for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into business software gives it a practical route to expanding enterprise adoption and paid Copilot subscriptions, according to Bank of America (BofA), which reiterated its 'buy' rating and $630 price objective. The bank's assessment followed an investor meeting with Jacob Andreou, Microsoft's executive vice-president of Copilot, to discuss the company's enterprise AI strategy, competitive position and product development priorities. BofA said Microsoft was focusing on improving Copilot's quality, expanding its capabilities and reducing AI costs to encourage wider adoption, while giving businesses greater control over spending and data. The company is targeting three categories of users: Starters, who access limited Copilot features included in existing Microsoft 365 plans; Subscribers, who pay for dedicated Copilot seats; and Advanced users, who use modules such as Autopilot and Code and pay according to AI consumption. Recent product developments include Today, designed to help users prioritize work, and Workspaces, which allow employees and AI agents to collaborate. The bank highlighted Work IQ, which connects Copilot to company information across emails, Teams conversations and documents, as a key competitive advantage because it provides business context for AI-generated responses and tasks. Microsoft also benefits from integrating Copilot into existing Office applications, allowing employees to use AI without requiring companies to replace their established software and workflows. Another advantage is Copilot's Auto mode, which selects between different AI models depending on task complexity, using less expensive models for simpler operations and more powerful systems when required. BofA believes this combination of business context, model flexibility and cost control can support broader enterprise adoption and growth in paid Copilot seats.

7df6e0085f.title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
7df6e0085f.summary: Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next. We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines. One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing. MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model. MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. The benchmark evaluates four components: Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided. Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another. Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements. Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties. b438a303cf.title: Why OpenAI’s latest model is obsessed with bells
b438a303cf.summary: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra keeps putting bells and “Bellwether” into AI-generated games and stories. The strange pattern may point to a broader AI problem. There’s an entire field dedicated to “the history, art and science of making and ringing bells.” It’s known as campanology, and its devotees have been around for centuries (see: The Ringing World and Bell News , two historical publications devoted to bells). OpenAI’s latest frontier model, GPT-6.2 Astra, is apparently among the discipline’s latest evangelists. When a user asks the model for help creating a game, app or image, it tends to weave bells into the story and setting—regardless of the initial prompt: church bells , call bells , even a fighting game character with a bell for an arm . Developer Theo Browne first noticed the phenomenon while testing an early version of 6.2 Astra, which was released on November 17. He’d asked the model to generate a video game level based on the 2019 adventure “Outer Wilds,” while his colleague requested one inspired by 2000’s “The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask.” “We both got water levels with music themes, specifically around bells,” Browne wrote. The similarities didn’t end there: “Both were named ‘Bellwether.’” Wharton Business School Associate Professor Ethan Mollick received an eerily similar response when he asked Astra for help vibe coding a puzzle game. The setting the model generated was a train terminal called “Bellwether Station” (not to be confused with a real-life rock band of the same name that’s “comprised mostly of lawyers”). Dozens more users have since chimed in with similar testimonies , suggesting that ChatGPT’s “bellwether” bias has existed for at least a few months, if not longer—and that the problem might even extend to competitors’ models. Mollick himself pointed out that an LLM adopting a quirky obsession isn’t uncommon, although the phenomenon keeps reappearing in ever stranger variations. Does the name Elias Thorne ring a bell? He’s the lighthouse keeper who haunts a disproportionate number of AI-generated stories, even though that name rarely appears in human-created works. Before that, ChatGPT couldn’t get enough of gremlins and goblins , supposedly because it overeagerly embraced a “nerdy personality.” While it isn’t yet clear what’s causing Astra’s current “campanophilia,” some users suspect it’s related to an engineering problem known as mode collapse , in which a model starts drawing from a limited set of learned patterns, restricting…

For tasks estimated at four to eight hours, the success rate rose from 13% to 35% over the same period. What is more, Aaron says that agent runtime per researcher has increased more than fivefold since June. At task level, agents succeeded on 79% of run-monitoring tasks and 72% of tasks answering technical questions. Success fell to 35% for launching training runs and 29% for building evaluation, reinforcement-learning and agent environments. Writing code for inference and serving stacks scored lowest at 25%. While these weaker categories could become bottlenecks to overall uplift, the broader performance gains are already driving output. 0b5d0afadc.summary: Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis, most famous problem in all of math An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology’s year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion By Joseph Howlett edited by Claire Cameron Levent Alpöge, a mathematician and employee at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claimed on Friday to have proven the most famous problem in all of mathematics using an LLM. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a statement posted on his website. The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order. If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. The conjecture has since become the North Star for the entire field of number theory, and is the most famous open problem in math. It’s one of the few open problems on which the Clay Mathematics Institute has placed a million-dollar bounty. Progress toward solving the Riemann hypothesis was so rare that most top experts spent little of their time actually working on it, because there was no obvious path to proving Riemann’s guess. The first chink in the problem’s armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI’s massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes. Now the long struggle appears over. Alpöge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn’t take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI’s mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. The announcement comes just a day after Anthropic's record-breaking debut on the stock market. 713cafea6c.summary: A sell-off in technology stocks intensified Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite’s gains for the year, as investors continued to pull money out of the once high-flying AI trade. The S&P 500 fell 3.6%, on track for a seventh day of losses – its longest losing streak since February 2020, when Wall Street started bracing for what became the Covid pandemic. The Nasdaq faced even steeper losses on Friday, dropping 5.3%. It is now down almost 2% for the year. Even Anthropic’s blockbuster stock market debut quickly lost its shine Friday, with shares in the AI lab plunging almost 10%. They’re now trading around $87.10, just above the company’s IPO of $83. “It’s a meltdown right now,” Arun Sundaram, senior vice president of investment strategy at CFRA Research, told CNN in an email. “So much bearish sentiment around tech and AI.” Why Anthropic’s blockbuster debut didn’t ease Wall Street’s AI fears Losses were less extreme for the Dow, which retreated 1.85%, cushioned by gains in stocks in other sectors, including healthcare and consumer staples. Even so, both it and the S&P 500 dipped into correction territory Friday, after sliding 10% from their respective peaks on August 5 and October 6. All together, all three indexes are on track for their worst week since early April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s tariff plans rocked global markets. Stocks associated with the AI trade have been in a serious rough patch for weeks now. But with Anthropic’s buzzy IPO now in the rear-view mirror, traders’ concerns about the broader industry are once again coming to the fore. Investors are grappling with a bevy of concerns, from uncertainty over how newly elected Democratic governors will impact the pace of the data center buildout to uncertainty about the future of Nvidia’s role in powering the AI industry’s growth after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. “There is a fear that maybe there is too much froth and enthusiasm in the tech bet given all the risks out there,” said David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management. Kelly noted that corrections are “inevitable” and there is “nothing particularly ominous” about a correction given how much US stocks have rallied in recent years. “This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu. At the moment, it looks like a mild cold, and it should be over in a week or two,” he said. 17a1392a9a.title: OpenAI Strengthens GPT-6.2 Astra Against Reasoning Extraction
17a1392a9a.summary: OpenAI on November 20, 2026 announced stronger defenses against adversarial distillation, reporting that the average success rate for adaptive attacks extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request fell from 54.0% on GPT-6 Astra with original safeguards to 0.2% on GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards. For extraction from the current request, the corresponding average fell from 22.9% to 0.9%, OpenAI reports. The adaptive black-box evaluation aggregates results across six attacker models, with automated red-teamers adjusting their approach as the system responds and seeing only what an external user would see. The strengthened protections cover GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, and selected improvements are also being applied to GPT-6 Astra . Protected reasoning is the intermediate chain-of-thought a model generates while working toward an answer. These traces can contain information omitted from final responses, making them especially valuable to adversarial distillation, which uses a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another system. The resulting model may reproduce dual-use capabilities without the safeguards that constrained the original. OpenAI’s internal study compared two training runs from the same pretrained student model, the learner in a setup where a teacher model produces the training data. One run used exact teacher reasoning traces; the other used the user-visible baseline of final responses, reasoning summaries and tool interactions. The fine-tuning data consisted primarily of Astra-level teacher trajectories on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Students were evaluated after supervised fine-tuning and again after lightweight reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments. After supervised fine-tuning, the exact-trace student generally outperformed the summary-trained student, OpenAI reports. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student scored higher at the largest tested inference budget on both reported benchmarks, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets. OpenAI interprets the results as evidence that protecting exact traces can limit cyber-capability transfer even when the underlying tasks are permitted under its usage policies, while saying it will continue studying transfer across different student models and training recipes. e8888a82f4.title: OpenAI introduces MedChemBench to test AI on medicinal chemistry
e8888a82f4.summary: The benchmark measures how well models handle drug discovery tasks, and even the top scorers are landing below 50% Fri 20 Nov 2026 · 14:07 EST · 2 min read OpenAI has introduced MedChemBench, a benchmark built to measure how well AI models handle the work of medicinal chemistry. The best score on its leaderboard is 49.7%. Medicinal chemistry is the discipline of designing and refining molecules that could become drugs. MedChemBench breaks that work into the kinds of tasks a chemist handles day to day. The benchmark covers interpreting chemical structures, predicting how potent or toxic a compound might be, choosing which candidate molecules to pursue, and mapping out routes to synthesize them. The research describes MedChemBench as an internal benchmark. In practice, that makes it a yardstick OpenAI uses to evaluate and refine its own models over time. As of late November 2026, OpenAI’s own models sit at the top of the MedChemBench leaderboard. GPT-6 Astra posted a score of 49.7%, while GPT-5.6 Sol came in at 48.3%. The more telling detail is the ceiling. Neither model clears half the benchmark, which the research attributes to persistent difficulty with consistent multi-step chemical reasoning. Daily. Free. f2618c8a6e.summary: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago. The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when. Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development. Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday. The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17. Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers. Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading. Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market. 316a00df68.title: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia legacy, Claude Fable 5.2 and Anthropic’s IPO, World Labs Releases Atlas to Developers
316a00df68.summary: I was saddened to hear about Jensen Huang resigning from Nvidia last week. Yes, Jensen made serious mistakes . At the same time, he is a brilliant leader that has done tremendous work growing AI — providing compute to power training and inference, championing open source, and more — while turning Nvidia into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Much has been written about Jensen’s unique contributions. I still remember years ago, when I made my early push to use GPUs for training neural networks . Jensen met this idea with a positive reception, and he provided resources to help my teams at Stanford and Google and — long before it was obvious to most people that this was a good idea — directed Nvidia to shift to serving deep learning workloads. This bold call was one of many that led to Nvidia’s success. I appreciate particularly that, to ensure Nvidia’s success, he focused on building a thriving AI ecosystem that enabled many other teams to flourish. In many large companies, there is a mantra that no one is irreplaceable. In hindsight, this statement certainly did not apply to Jensen. Nvidia’s board may yet reinstate him as CEO, but if not, I wonder what future contributions he could have made to Nvidia that we will miss out on — and never know we missed. I hope everyone will see in Jensen’s critical role a refutation of the idea that people are replaceable. We should try to build teams that are robust enough to survive any individual’s departure. But at the same time, we should try to make contributions that others will look back on and understand were indispensable. Jensen is a hero of the AI world. When I wrote the blurb for his TIME 100 Award , I remember thinking there was so much more I could have written about him than would fit in the word count. I’m confident he will continue to make huge contributions. Let us all take inspiration from his example of the difference a single person can make and strive to contribute as much as we can. a52262e0f6.title: Amicus Brief in In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation
a52262e0f6.summary: Today, General Counsel and Senior Fellow Tim Hwang, with help from Research Fellow Sam Roland, filed a proposed amicus brief in support of OpenAI in In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation . General AI capabilities already serve important national security purposes. Over the last several years, the Government has acquired and adapted commercial frontier models for intelligence analysis, cyber defense, operational planning, and decision support. Both branches of government understand the importance of this new technological paradigm: Congress has supported it by tying defense AI to training and data and the executive by proclaiming rapid access to current models as one of its top national security priorities. Copyright protects authors for a simple reason: their work advances knowledge and culture. Fair use serves the same end. It preserves room for new uses that benefit the public without displacing the expression copyright protects. But factor four of the fair use test is not limited to an accounting of the copyright holder’s potential lost revenue. Under Google LLC v. Oracle Am., Inc. , courts may also consider the public benefits that copying enables, particularly where the use puts copyrighted works toward new productive ends. To the extent AI training enables the creation of new knowledge, expression, software, and other capabilities, those benefits bear on factor four’s assessment of the use’s market effects. That reasoning supports a novel application here: considering the national-security value of capabilities that enable new analysis, software, and other productive work. The link between copying a newspaper article and developing national-security capabilities lies in the training process. During pretraining, models identify shared patterns across a broad corpus of information. Learning those patterns helps develop language, synthesis, translation, coding, and reasoning capabilities. Requiring permission for the challenged training could impair those benefits if it materially restricts access to useful training data. Removing useful sources from training data can reduce capabilities used by downstream systems, which could include the national security systems the Government acquires and adapts. Under Oracle , those public benefits belong in the factor-four balance alongside cognizable market harm.

Get their code through, and then that kind of alleviates that relationship barrier between industry that doesn’t have a relationship with the government,” Acting CIO of the Army Gabe Chiulli said Friday at the Annual Data Forum, presented by AFCEA International. “They get the government check, and that code gets moved into an IL5 environment after it gets through all the different checks, and says, ‘hey, you are now capable of essentially selling your product or distributing your product into a secure Army enclave,’” Chiulli added. He said he’s working with the other military department CIOs to try to establish “reciprocity” so that they don’t have to build their own systems for this type of process. Vendors with a Defense Department Common Access Card can log in to Gatekeeper to use the system. But, Chiulli noted, officials are working to open it up more widely and allow companies to access it via the Login.gov platform. At Friday’s conference, DefenseScoop asked the Army CIO about the timeline for integrating AI models into the Gatekeeper initiative. “I’m going to put it into the next quarter,” Chiulli replied. “I think what it’ll be is a phased approach of different commercialized models. 7718daf855.title: Microsoft outage: Does Microsoft owe you money? What to know.
7718daf855.summary: Microsoft's massive, productivity-destroying software outage appears to be receding as of Friday morning, but that's only the start of the process for businesses looking to get some of their Office 365 money back. Several important enterprise software products, such as Outlook and Teams, were functionally offline for many users on Thursday and into Friday. Since Office 365 is a service businesses have to pay for, it raises the question: Can those businesses receive some form of compensation from Microsoft for the time lost? The answer to that question is nuanced. Let's get into it. According to helpful resources like these explainers from Quartz and Office Watch , the short answer is no; Microsoft does not owe anyone money as a result of this outage. But that doesn't mean the company doesn't owe any compensation , as it offers credits (essentially a reduction on the next bill) in the event of an outage. One important thing to note: You have to request a credit. Microsoft doesn't offer them automatically. Purchasing Microsoft's software suite involves a service-level agreement (SLA). This SLA includes provisions related to outages and compensation. In this case, Microsoft's SLA promises 99.9 percent uptime each month for each piece of software in the suite, such as OneDrive and Outlook. If any of those services fall below the 99.9 percent threshold, it's possible to claim a credit. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile "Possible" is the key word here, though, as both Quartz and Office Watch make it very clear that Microsoft is extremely strict about how it calculates downtime in these instances. The actual math is too complicated to fully get into here, but Microsoft counts downtime in terms of "user minutes," or the amount of time the services were down multiplied by the number of users demonstrably affected. Credits are also prorated depending on how much uptime was lost, so a small amount of downtime might only be worth a 25 or 50 percent credit. Where this gets even more complicated is that Microsoft calculates credits according to each individual service, not the entire software bundle. If you only lost service time in Outlook, but other parts of the Office 365 suite worked, you'd only get a small credit for Outlook. All of this is to say that, depending on the size of the affected business and the amount of downtime it experienced, one of these credits could be worth only a few measly dollars. To be very…

Human resources management freshman Bella Greene woke up sick the morning of the Microsoft Outlook outage on Nov. 12, so she emailed her professor to say she wouldn't make it to class and went back to sleep, assuming her message went through. Gavin Newsom on Thursday released a wide-ranging set of policy recommendations to mitigate risks from artificial intelligence, including letting state officials order an immediate emergency shutdown of AI systems they deem dangerous. Other recommendations would mandate that independent auditors test AI models and establish safety and security standards. The shutdown power, popularly known as a “kill switch,” would apply when companies like ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic refuse to take action to contain systems that go awry. The recommendations were drawn up by a panel of experts brought together by Newsom earlier this fall , following high-profile cyberattacks by AI agents on governments, banks, and private companies. The governor touted them as a blueprint for state legislation during a recent visit to Washington, according to a report in Politico . Newsom, who is widely expected to mount a presidential run, said the state is filling a vacuum left by a lack of AI rules at the federal level. “Instead of protecting the public, Donald Trump shrugs his shoulders and leaves AI regulation up to the companies themselves,” he said in a press release announcing the recommendations. California is home to some of the largest AI companies in the world, and the California Legislature has passed more bills to regulate AI than any other state in the country. Newsom signed dozens of bills passed by the California Legislature into law in September to do things like protect kids , workers , and people living near data centers from AI and related impacts. He also accelerated implementation of laws to create an AI auditor registry and set standards for auditors . Legislators can propose new bills when they return to Sacramento on Dec. 7. The recommendations come the same week as a lawsuit by Attorney General Rob Bonta against OpenAI in an attempt to hold the company legally responsible for cybersecurity attacks carried out by agents made by the company. 9eb81845eb.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI helped solve a 167-year-old math mystery
9eb81845eb.summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used Claude to solve one of mathematics’ most famous unsolved problems—a claim that could mark a historic breakthrough for artificial intelligence if it withstands scrutiny. The Riemann hypothesis , which has stumped mathematicians since 1859, concerns the distribution of prime numbers, the building blocks of arithmetic. On Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that he believes he and the company’s AI system have developed a proof. Independent mathematicians have yet to verify the result, but one leading expert expressed optimism. “If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics, establishing one of the great mysteries of the subject,” James Maynard, the Regius Professor of Mathematics at the University of Oxford and a 2022 Fields Medal winner, told IBM Think in an interview. “This result really stands out, even in the context of all the recent AI breakthroughs.” Prime numbers are numbers divisible only by 1 and themselves, such as 2, 3 and 5, and the Riemann hypothesis predicts a remarkably precise pattern in how they are distributed. Proving it would resolve a question that has baffled mathematicians since 1859 and deepen their understanding of the hidden structure of numbers. The Clay Mathematics Institute includes the hypothesis among its seven Millennium Prize Problems , each carrying a USD 1 million award. The claim follows a string of recent AI-assisted advances in mathematics, including work on longstanding conjectures and difficult theoretical problems. In a September interview with IBM Think , Fields Medal winner Terence Tao warned that AI could produce solutions faster than mathematicians could understand the discoveries behind them. In his announcement, Alpöge said the proposed proof also covered the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions. Rather than publish a conventional mathematical paper, Alpöge released his argument in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks mathematical reasoning step by step. He acknowledged that the argument remained extraordinarily long and difficult to read. The proposed proof would go much further than an earlier AI-assisted mathematical breakthrough, according to Youness Lamzouri ⁠, a professor of mathematics at the University of Lorraine in France. df13cf8e4e.summary: On the afternoon of Nov. 12, senior Max Flecchia was waiting for a response to his email regarding an important career move. “I didn’t know how long it would take. I was being held up from potentially scoring a job interview,” he said. He was not alone. Multiple students and faculty members were waiting on emails all day, and unable to send any themselves. The thing holding them up? A worldwide shutdown of Microsoft. Multiple services powered by Microsoft 365, including Teams, Copilot, and Exchange Online, were inaccessible and not working properly. Exchange Online is the cloud-based background service that manages and stores the emails, contacts, and calendars associated with Outlook, meaning people were unable to send or receive emails as usual. Junior Brigid Milligan said while her schoolwork wasn’t necessarily affected, her job at an animal hospital was, as the staff was unable to obtain records for some pets. Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report (PIR) stated the cause was an old Windows server defect. Increased traffic and reduced infrastructure capacity were also responsible for the disruption. Microsoft’s investigation of the outage uncovered that the previously undetected defect was introduced through a Windows update to the network in July of this year. However, it had gone undetected due to the fact that the system tests were being run in a way that would not cause the issue to arise, according to an article published by data analyst Sebastian Castellanos. The PIR said the defect was the internal Windows process experienced lock contention, which occurs when certain sessions need the same protected database at the same time and begin to wait on one another. This caused the central processing unit and the memory to become “exhausted,” making the servers’ response times slower or even completely unresponsive. Another factor of the Microsoft outage was the digital traffic was automatically redirected to the primary gateway that is shared with Exchange Online as opposed to an alternative networking gateway, according to the PIR. One final factor Microsoft said contributed to the outage was the server capacity being 14% unavailable from an unrelated, unspecified issue from the previous day. The increased workload from these problems on an already affected infrastructure triggered over 80% of servers to stop responding within two hours. Microsoft said the immediate recovery was difficult because the servers continued to shut down repeatedly…

a53e8ede7e.title: Combatting adversarial distillation
a53e8ede7e.summary: How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry. As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked. We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry. Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity. We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards. Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why . a97183d7be.title: Gold tongues and hundreds of stone coffins uncovered in ancient Egyptian cemetery
a97183d7be.summary: Egyptian archaeologists have uncovered hundreds of stone coffins and tongue-shaped pieces of gold at an ancient cemetery in the northern province of Menoufia. The discovery was made at Tell Kom Abu Billo, within the site of the ancient city of Terenouthis, the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said. The city stood near the eastern entrance to Wadi El Natrun, a valley west of the Nile Delta known for its deposits of natron, a naturally occurring mixture of salts that embalmers used to dry bodies before wrapping them. Human sacrifice in ancient Egypt uncovered by modern forensic science Earlier excavations at Kom Abu Billo uncovered remains of the city and a temple dedicated to the goddess Hathor. The gold tongues indicate another aspect of ancient Egyptian beliefs about death: the idea that the dead would need to speak in the afterlife. Archaeologists also recovered jewellery, scarab amulets and small figurines buried with the dead, and found two falcon burials. Many of the stone coffins were clustered in an open courtyard, a concentration that the Supreme Council of Antiquities said had not been seen before at the site. Some were missing their lids and others had been shattered by earlier looting and quarrying. The team also found pottery coffins, remnants of wooden coffins and tombs built from mudbrick. The burials span the end of Egypt’s Late Period to the early Roman era. Preliminary studies suggest much of the cemetery dates to the third and second centuries BC, when the Ptolemaic dynasty ruled Egypt. The objects left with the dead offer clues to who was buried there. Based on an initial study of the grave goods, the council believes the cemetery mainly served middle class people. Excavations are continuing, and the full extent of the burial ground is not yet known.

A defence source in Riyadh added that the tactic also mirrors Iranian operations against Bahrain, where individual missiles were used to force defenders to activate their systems and expend interceptors. “Air-defence success cannot be measured solely by the number of missiles intercepted – it must also be measured by whether the country can keep operating normally,” he added. There have also been suggestions that dwindling Houthi stocks, with an estimated 100 to 200 ballistic missiles remaining, could explain the preference for individual attacks against civilian targets rather than saturation strikes. As we wrote recently , the problems are far more than just cybersecurity, though AI means hackers can discover and exploit bugs like never before. Infrastructure is decrepit. Maintenance is deferred. Exhausted, too-small teams of IT workers aren't up to this level of chaos. But there's another explanation that's perhaps underappreciated: one big downside of Claude Code, the marquee product that has given Anthropic ( ANT ) its trillion-dollar valuation. The problem is best explained by someone who would know best: a prominent Anthropic engineer (and former Google engineer) who works on Claude Code as a member of the technical staff, Addy Osmani, whose treatise on " comprehension debt " bounced around the software engineering community in March — and is even more relevant today. What Osmani highlights isn't really a weakness in Claude Code, but in how companies and engineering teams use it. The gist: AI can write code faster than we can review it. The speed is a great benefit, but it's also a curse, as myriad companies pivot from writing code to overseeing teams of AI agents that complain less and write more. As Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week , the company's engineers "build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product." Traditionally, the laborious process of checking other people's code is how software engineers internalize why systems are designed the way they are, and why decisions from earlier in a project might be meaningful today. But reviewing the entirety of AI code isn't feasible given how fast we can produce it now. It's too unwieldy, and this represents a massive bottleneck for progress. Tests, AI review, and spending less time reviewing can be effective. But they've removed layers of verification, and ultimately comprehension, which is disappearing, Osmani explains. Friday’s vote was particularly significant because council members used colour-coded ballots for only the second time in the selection process. The system distinguishes votes cast by the five permanent members – the US, Britain, France, Russia and China – from those of the 10 elected members. Any of the five permanent members can effectively block a candidate from taking the post, making its opposition a major obstacle even for contenders with broad support. The council first used coloured ballots on October 16 before returning to regular voting for the next two rounds. Friday marked the first time that Ms Nusseibeh and Mr Sinirlioglu faced colour-coded ballots, which offered a clearer indication of whether either could secure the support needed to win. 19bfc5f525.summary: A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic says he used the company's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems. The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work. Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday . The proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research. The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most important in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI. Alpoge said that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved. "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems , selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those. "This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, said in a statement quoted by news agency AP. He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics." "But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult." Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1. The hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.
